title: Caffeine and Alcohol: Does Coffee Sober You Up? What Really Happens
excerpt: Does coffee sober you up? How caffeine and alcohol interact, why energy drinks make you a 'wide-awake drunk,' espresso martini caffeine, sleep, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Does coffee sober you up? How caffeine and alcohol interact, the wide-awake drunk risk, energy drinks, espresso martinis, sleep, and hangover tips.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** caffeine does not sober you up. It doesn't lower your blood alcohol, it doesn't speed up how fast your liver clears alcohol, and it doesn't restore your judgment or reaction time. What it does is make you feel more awake. That gap between how alert you feel and how impaired you actually are is the main risk of mixing the two, and it's why researchers call the result being "wide-awake drunk." A cup of coffee with dinner and a glass of wine is not a problem for most healthy adults. Energy drinks mixed with spirits, several espresso martinis in a row, or coffee chugged before driving home are where things go wrong.

**The quick rules:** Don't use coffee or energy drinks to "fix" being drunk, and never use them to decide you're fine to drive. Count the caffeine in cocktails like espresso martinis and vodka Red Bulls, because it adds up fast. Keep total caffeine under about 400 mg a day, the level the FDA describes as generally not linked to harmful effects in healthy adults. Stop caffeine by mid-afternoon on nights you plan to drink, so you don't stack two sleep disruptors. And the morning after, a normal cup of coffee is fine if you're a regular coffee drinker, but it won't cure a hangover.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor before mixing caffeine and alcohol if** you have a heart rhythm problem, high blood pressure, an anxiety or panic disorder, acid reflux or ulcers, or you are pregnant. Also ask your pharmacist if you take stimulant medication for ADHD, certain antidepressants, or antibiotics such as ciprofloxacin, which can slow how fast your body clears caffeine. **Get emergency help (call 911 in the US) if** someone who has been drinking has chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat that won't settle, trouble breathing, confusion, seizures, vomiting while drowsy, or can't be woken up. Coffee will not help them.

## What Happens in Your Body When You Mix Caffeine and Alcohol

The two drugs work on different systems, and they don't cancel each other out. They just pull your brain in opposite directions on some things and leave other things untouched.

### How caffeine wakes you up

Throughout the day your brain builds up a chemical called **adenosine**. As it accumulates, it binds to receptors that make you feel drowsy. That's part of what "sleep pressure" is. Caffeine has a similar shape to adenosine, so it sits in those receptors and blocks them. The adenosine is still there, but your brain can't read the signal, so you feel more alert.

Caffeine takes about 30 to 60 minutes to reach its peak effect, and its half-life (the time it takes your body to clear half of it) is usually somewhere around 3 to 7 hours in healthy adults. That range is wide because genetics, smoking, pregnancy, birth control pills, and some medicines all change how fast you break it down.

### How alcohol slows you down

Alcohol is a depressant. It boosts the brain's main calming signal (GABA) and dampens its main excitatory signal (glutamate). That's why it relaxes you at first, then slows your reaction time, loosens your inhibitions, and eventually makes you sleepy. Alcohol also raises adenosine activity, which is one reason you get drowsy after a few drinks. Our guide on [why alcohol makes you sleepy](/never-hungover/why-does-alcohol-make-you-sleepy) goes into that in more detail.

### Why they don't cancel out

Caffeine mostly counters the **sleepiness** part of being drunk. It does much less for the **impairment** part. Your liver breaks down alcohol at roughly the same steady pace no matter what else you drink, so your blood alcohol concentration (BAC) stays the same. Your coordination, judgment, and ability to stop yourself from doing something risky stay impaired too.

So the combination removes one of your body's most useful warning signs. Feeling tired is how your body tells you to stop drinking and go home. When caffeine masks that signal, you feel like you have more in the tank than you do.

## Does Coffee Sober You Up?

No. This is the single most common myth about caffeine and alcohol, and it's worth being completely clear about it.

- **Coffee doesn't lower your BAC.** Only time does that. Your body clears alcohol at roughly one standard drink per hour, give or take, and nothing you drink speeds that up in a meaningful way. Our guide on [how long alcohol stays in your system](/never-hungover/how-long-does-alcohol-stay-in-your-system) explains the timeline.
- **Coffee doesn't fix your reaction time or judgment.** Lab studies have consistently found that caffeine can make people *feel* less drunk and can improve some simple measures like basic reaction speed, but it does not restore the kind of control you need to stop yourself from acting on impulse.
- **Coffee can make you more confident than you should be.** This is the dangerous part. Someone who feels alert after two coffees may decide they're fine to drive when they're not.

One frequently cited lab study by Marczinski and Fillmore (published in *Experimental and Clinical Psychopharmacology* in 2006) looked at exactly this. Adding caffeine to alcohol reduced some of the slowing effects of alcohol, but it did not reduce alcohol's effect on people's ability to hold back a response. In plain terms, people moved faster but didn't get better at stopping themselves. Other researchers have reached similar conclusions, including work testing caffeinated beer in driving simulators, which did not find that caffeine made drunk driving performance safe.

**The bottom line on sobering up:** if you've had too much to drink, the only things that help are time, water, food, and sleep. If you need to get home, use a ride service, a sober driver, or public transport. Coffee is not a safety plan.

## The "Wide-Awake Drunk" Problem

Researchers have used the phrase "wide-awake drunk" to describe what happens when caffeine hides alcohol's sedating effects. It isn't just a catchy label. It points to three real risks.

### 1. You may drink more than you planned

When you don't feel tired, it's easier to keep going. Survey research has repeatedly found that people who mix alcohol with energy drinks tend to drink more per session and report more binge drinking than people who drink alcohol alone. Surveys like this can't prove the energy drink *causes* the extra drinking (people who like to party hard may simply be more likely to reach for energy drinks), but the pattern has been consistent enough that public health agencies take it seriously.

Energy drinks are the extreme case here, with large caffeine doses plus sugar and other stimulants. Our [energy drinks and alcohol](/never-hungover/energy-drinks-and-alcohol) guide covers vodka Red Bulls and Jägerbombs specifically; this page is about caffeine in general, including coffee, tea, and espresso martinis.

### 2. Risky decisions go up

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has a fact sheet on alcohol and caffeine. It notes that drinkers who mix alcohol with energy drinks are more likely to report binge drinking and are more likely than drinkers who don't mix them to report riding with a driver who had been drinking and other alcohol-related harms. Again, that's an association rather than proof of cause, but it lines up with what the lab research on impulse control would predict.

### 3. Your usual stopping signals don't work

Most people rely on feeling drowsy, heavy, or clumsy to know they've had enough. Caffeine dulls the drowsiness, and the other signals are easy to ignore when you feel energetic. That's why mixed caffeine-alcohol drinks are so often tied to the nights people say got away from them.

## Energy Drinks and Alcohol

Energy drinks deserve their own section because they're the most common way people combine the two, and the doses are higher than most people realize.

### Why the FDA stepped in

In November 2010, the US Food and Drug Administration sent warning letters to several companies that sold pre-mixed caffeinated alcoholic beverages, the best known being the original Four Loko. The FDA said that caffeine added to malt alcoholic drinks was an "unsafe food additive" in that setting, citing concerns about the "wide-awake drunk" effect and reports of serious harm. The companies reformulated, and pre-mixed caffeinated alcohol largely disappeared from US shelves.

That action only covered drinks sold already mixed. Nothing stops people from mixing their own, which is exactly what a vodka Red Bull or a Jägerbomb is.

### How much caffeine is in common mixed drinks

Caffeine content varies by brand and recipe, so treat these as rough figures from typical label values:

| Drink | Approximate caffeine |
|---|---|
| Standard 8.4 oz can of Red Bull | About 80 mg |
| 16 oz energy drink (many brands) | Roughly 150 to 300 mg |
| Shot of espresso | About 60 to 75 mg |
| Espresso martini (one shot of espresso plus coffee liqueur) | Often roughly 60 to 100 mg |
| 8 oz brewed coffee | About 80 to 100 mg, sometimes more |
| Irish coffee (about 6 oz coffee) | About 60 to 90 mg |
| 12 oz cola (rum and Coke) | About 30 to 45 mg |
| Coffee liqueur alone (1.5 oz) | Usually small, often under 15 mg |

Three or four vodka Red Bulls can put you near or over 400 mg of caffeine in an evening, on top of whatever coffee you had during the day. At that point you're getting the side effects of both: jitters, a fast heartbeat, anxiety, and a stomach that's being irritated from two directions.

### Heart rhythm concerns

Both alcohol and high doses of caffeine can trigger palpitations, and heavy drinking on its own can set off an irregular heart rhythm (doctors sometimes call it "holiday heart"). For most healthy people a moderate amount of caffeine doesn't cause dangerous rhythms. But if you have a known heart condition, high blood pressure, or a history of atrial fibrillation, the combination of binge drinking and large amounts of caffeine is a reasonable thing to avoid. If your heart races or flutters after a night out, our guide on [heart racing after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking) covers when it's normal and when to get it checked.

## Espresso Martinis, Irish Coffee, and Other Coffee Cocktails

Coffee cocktails are having a moment, especially the espresso martini. They are a gentler version of the same combination, but the same principles apply.

**One espresso martini** contains about as much caffeine as a single shot of espresso, plus around one and a half to two standard drinks' worth of alcohol depending on the pour. For most people one is fine. The trouble starts when espresso martinis become the drink of the night. Four of them can add up to several hundred milligrams of caffeine and six or more standard drinks, often in a sweet, easy-to-drink form that goes down fast.

**Irish coffee and spiked coffees** usually have more caffeine than an espresso martini (because they use a full cup of coffee) and less alcohol per glass. They're usually sipped slowly, which helps.

**Rum and Coke** and other cola mixers have modest caffeine per glass, but they add sugar and can still keep you up later than you'd like.

The night-after effect is worth knowing too. Coffee cocktails often mean late-evening caffeine, which collides with alcohol's own sleep disruption. Our [espresso martini hangover](/never-hungover/espresso-martini-hangover) guide looks at why that particular drink seems to produce rough mornings.

## Caffeine, Alcohol, and Sleep

This is where the combination quietly does the most everyday damage, even for moderate drinkers.

Alcohol helps you fall asleep but breaks up the second half of the night. As your body finishes processing it, you get a rebound effect: lighter sleep, more waking, and less REM sleep (the dreaming stage tied to mood and memory). Caffeine does its own damage. Because of its long half-life, a coffee at 4 p.m. can still be partly active at midnight, making it harder to reach deep sleep.

Put the two together and you get a night where you crash into bed, sleep badly, and wake up exhausted. That poor sleep is a big part of why the next day feels so bad. Hangover researchers consider disrupted sleep one of the main contributors to hangover fatigue and brain fog.

A few practical points:

- **Set a caffeine cutoff on drinking days.** Stopping by early to mid-afternoon gives your body time to clear most of it.
- **Skip the late coffee cocktail if sleep matters.** An espresso martini at 11 p.m. is caffeine right before bed.
- **Don't drink alcohol to "come down" from caffeine.** Using one drug to cancel the other tends to mean more of both.

If you regularly wake at 3 a.m. after drinking, our guide on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) explains what's happening and what helps.

## Does Coffee Help a Hangover?

It depends on what's causing your misery and whether you're a regular coffee drinker.

### When coffee can help

- **If you drink coffee every day, skipping it can make your hangover worse.** Caffeine withdrawal causes headaches, fatigue, irritability, and trouble concentrating, which overlap heavily with hangover symptoms. A normal morning cup can head off that extra layer.
- **It can ease grogginess.** Caffeine can take the edge off the tiredness, though it doesn't fix the cause.
- **It's part of some headache treatments.** Caffeine is added to certain over-the-counter headache pills because it can make pain relievers work a little better. That doesn't make coffee a hangover cure, but it explains why some people feel it helps their head.

### When coffee can make things worse

- **Upset stomach and heartburn.** Both alcohol and coffee can irritate the stomach lining and relax the valve that keeps acid down. If you already feel queasy or have acid reflux, coffee on an empty stomach may tip you over. See our guide on [heartburn after drinking](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking).
- **Anxiety and a jumpy heart.** Many people feel anxious the day after drinking (sometimes called "[hangxiety](/never-hungover/hangxiety-complete-guide-2026-supplements-research)"). Caffeine can amplify that jittery feeling. If you're already shaky or your heart is pounding, go easy.
- **Dehydration worries are mostly overstated.** Caffeine has a mild diuretic effect, but for regular coffee drinkers a normal cup doesn't meaningfully dehydrate you. Alcohol is the bigger factor. Still, coffee isn't a substitute for water.

### What there is no good evidence for

There is no good evidence that coffee speeds up hangover recovery, clears alcohol by-products like acetaldehyde, or protects your liver from a night of drinking. Long-term studies have linked regular coffee drinking with lower rates of some liver diseases, but that research is about years of habits, not a single morning, and it isn't a license to drink more.

**A sensible hangover-morning approach:** water first, then food, then your normal amount of coffee if you're a regular drinker. Don't double up. If coffee usually upsets your stomach when you're hungover, try tea, which has less caffeine.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

You're more likely to run into trouble with caffeine and alcohol together if you:

- **Have a heart condition**, a history of palpitations or atrial fibrillation, or high blood pressure
- **Have an anxiety or panic disorder**, since both caffeine and alcohol withdrawal can trigger symptoms
- **Have acid reflux, gastritis, or ulcers**
- **Take stimulant medication** (such as for ADHD) or medicines that slow caffeine clearance; ask a pharmacist
- **Are pregnant or trying to get pregnant**, when official guidance is to avoid alcohol and limit caffeine
- **Are young or a newer drinker**, because you have less sense of your own limits, and energy-drink mixes are popular in college settings
- **Plan to drive.** No amount of caffeine makes it safe to drive after drinking

If any of these fit, a short conversation with a doctor or pharmacist is worth it. For a broader look at how alcohol interacts with medicines and supplements, see our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## How to Mix Them More Sensibly If You Do

Plenty of people enjoy an Irish coffee or a single espresso martini without any problems. If you're going to combine caffeine and alcohol, these habits keep the risks low:

1. **Count caffeine like you count drinks.** Keep the day's total under about 400 mg, including morning coffee, tea, soda, and pre-workout.
2. **Limit caffeinated cocktails to one or two.** Switch to non-caffeinated drinks after that.
3. **Avoid energy drink mixers.** They carry the highest caffeine doses and the strongest link to heavier drinking.
4. **Decide your drink limit before you start.** Don't rely on feeling tired to tell you when to stop, because caffeine will hide that feeling.
5. **Alternate with water.** It slows your pace and helps the morning after.
6. **Eat beforehand.** Food slows alcohol absorption and protects your stomach from both drinks.
7. **Have a ride plan.** Decide how you're getting home before your first drink, not after.
8. **Watch your friends.** Someone mixing energy drinks with shots may seem fine and then crash hard once the caffeine wears off and the alcohol doesn't.

## When to Get Help Right Away

The biggest danger with caffeine and alcohol is that the caffeine can make someone with a lot of alcohol in their system look more okay than they are. When the caffeine wears off, the full effect of the alcohol can hit at once.

**Call 911 (or your local emergency number) if someone who has been drinking:**

- Can't be woken up or keeps drifting in and out
- Is confused, has slow or irregular breathing, or has pale, blue, or cold skin
- Is vomiting while very drowsy (lay them on their side so they don't choke)
- Has a seizure
- Has chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle with rest, or fainting

Don't give someone coffee and leave them to "sleep it off." Stay with them, keep them on their side, and get help. Alcohol poisoning is a medical emergency, and caffeine does nothing to treat it.

**See a doctor soon (not an emergency) if** you often get palpitations, chest discomfort, or strong anxiety when you drink, or if you notice you need caffeine to keep drinking or alcohol to come down from caffeine on a regular basis. Those are worth talking through with someone who knows your health history.

## A Better Way to Protect the Next Morning

Coffee helps you feel awake. It doesn't help your body deal with the alcohol itself. If you're searching for caffeine and alcohol because you want to feel better the next day, the steps with the best evidence are simple: drink less and drink more slowly, eat a real meal, alternate with water, and protect your sleep by cutting caffeine early. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) walks through those habits.

Some people also add a supplement. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and on how the brain responds to alcohol. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data, so it's promising rather than proven. It does **not** sober you up, it doesn't make it safe to drive, and it doesn't change anything about the caffeine side of the equation. If you want to try it alongside sensible drinking habits, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing and amounts, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## The Bottom Line

- Caffeine does not sober you up. It doesn't lower your blood alcohol or fix your judgment. It only makes you feel more alert.
- That false alertness can lead people to drink more, take more risks, and misjudge whether they can drive.
- Energy drink mixers carry the most caffeine and the strongest link to heavy drinking. Coffee cocktails like espresso martinis are milder, but they add up if you have several.
- Keep total caffeine under about 400 mg a day, stop it by mid-afternoon on drinking nights, and decide your drink limit in advance.
- The morning after, a normal cup of coffee is fine for regular coffee drinkers and can prevent a withdrawal headache, but water, food, and sleep do the real work.
- If someone who has been drinking can't stay awake, is breathing slowly, or has chest pain, call 911. Coffee won't help.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is it safe to mix caffeine and alcohol?**

A small amount, like one Irish coffee or one espresso martini, is unlikely to harm a healthy adult. The risk rises with larger amounts, especially energy drinks mixed with spirits. Caffeine hides alcohol's sleepiness without reducing your impairment, which can lead you to drink more and take more risks. If you have a heart condition, high blood pressure, anxiety, or reflux, or you take stimulant medication, talk to your doctor first.

**Does coffee sober you up?**

No. Coffee doesn't lower your blood alcohol concentration or speed up how fast your liver clears alcohol. It can make you feel more awake, but your judgment, coordination, and impulse control stay impaired. Only time sobers you up, at roughly one standard drink per hour, though this varies from person to person. Never use coffee to decide you're fine to drive.

**Why are energy drinks and alcohol a bad combination?**

Energy drinks contain a lot of caffeine, often 80 to 300 mg per can, which masks the drowsiness that normally tells you to stop drinking. Surveys have linked mixing alcohol with energy drinks to more binge drinking and more alcohol-related harms. The FDA warned makers of pre-mixed caffeinated alcoholic drinks in 2010, and those products were reformulated. Mixing your own at a bar carries the same concerns.

**How much caffeine is in an espresso martini?**

Usually roughly 60 to 100 mg, mostly from the shot of espresso, with a small amount from coffee liqueur. That's similar to a cup of coffee. One is fine for most people, but several espresso martinis add up to a lot of caffeine and alcohol, and having them late at night can wreck your sleep.

**Does coffee help a hangover?**

It can help a little in specific ways. If you drink coffee every day, skipping it can add a caffeine-withdrawal headache on top of your hangover, so your usual cup can help. It also eases grogginess. But there is no good evidence that coffee speeds up hangover recovery, and it can make nausea, heartburn, and anxiety worse. Drink water and eat something first.

**How long should I wait between caffeine and alcohol?**

There's no official rule. Caffeine stays partly active for several hours, so many people find it helps to stop caffeine by early to mid-afternoon on days they plan to drink. That keeps the two from overlapping much and protects your sleep, which is one of the biggest factors in how you feel the next day.

**Can caffeine and alcohol cause heart palpitations?**

Yes, both can, and together they can make palpitations more likely, especially with binge drinking or large amounts of caffeine. For most healthy people this is uncomfortable rather than dangerous. Get emergency care for chest pain, fainting, shortness of breath, or a racing or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle with rest, and see a doctor if palpitations happen often.

**Does DHM work with coffee or energy drinks?**

There's no good evidence that DHM changes how caffeine and alcohol interact. DHM is studied for effects on alcohol metabolism, mostly in animal and lab research with limited human data. It doesn't sober you up, doesn't make it safe to drive, and doesn't offset the risks of energy drink mixers. Sensible drinking habits matter far more than any supplement.
